Saad, a fourth grader, obtained a percen: Saad, a fourth grader, obtained a percentile rank of 50 on a standardized reading test, placing him exactly in the middle of his peers. This is norm-referenced information, and it does not point to a problem. On a criterion-referenced test, however, his teacher noticed that he could not distinguish between letters that share the same shape and differ only in their dots, such as ب (bāʾ), ت (tāʾ) and ث (thāʾ). The first test does not reveal this, yet it is precisely what the teacher needs to know in order to decide what to teach tomorrow.

In Arabic, it is more useful to analyze: In Arabic, it is more useful to analyze an error from two angles: decoding and morphological structure. Take Ghadeer's reading of “سافرَ” (sāfara) for “سفَر” (safar). The two words share a root (s-f-r), so the root letters are intact; the error lies in the pattern. She read a word on the faʿal pattern as though it were on the fāʿala pattern, adding a long vowel that is not in the text and turning the noun into a verb familiar to her. The diagnostic questions here are: Does she read short vowels and long vowels as written? Does she substitute a familiar word from the same root for the printed word? Does this recur in both vowelized and unvowelized passages? Among the most important things a teache: Among the most important things a teacher should know is that a child who speaks in his own dialect does not have a disorder. Children learn to talk from their families and pronounce words as the people around them do. A child who says “گلم” (galam, “pen”) in a community where everyone pronounces the qaf as a g is speaking entirely correctly by the standard of his dialect.
